questions.q: Define verbal irony and give one example from "The Luncheon" where the woman's spoken words contradict her actions.
questions.a: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says one thing but means the opposite, often to criticize or amuse. In "The Luncheon," the woman repeatedly says "I never eat more than one thing for luncheon" while proceeding to order and consume caviar, salmon, asparagus, ice cream, coffee, and a peach — a clear contradiction between her words and actions. A wrong answer (e.g., defining it as "sarcasm" or giving a situational irony example) reveals confusion between irony types and inability to distinguish verbal irony from other forms.

questions.q: Explain the difference between situational irony and dramatic irony using two distinct moments from the story.
questions.a: Situational irony arises when the outcome of a situation is starkly different from what was expected: the author expects a modest luncheon (15 francs) but faces a bill that leaves him penniless for the month. Dramatic irony occurs when the reader knows something a character does not: we know the author is calculating every franc and planning to claim his money was stolen, while the woman remains oblivious to his financial panic. A wrong answer that swaps the definitions or cites the same moment for both reveals inability to distinguish expectation-reversal (situational) from knowledge-asymmetry (dramatic).

questions.q: The author describes the woman's teeth as "white and large and even... more teeth than were necessary for any practical purpose." Identify the literary device and explain what this description symbolizes about her character.
questions.a: This is symbolism. The excessive, prominent teeth symbolize her predatory, consuming nature — she "devours" not just food but the author's resources, hospitality, and dignity. The phrase "more than necessary for any practical purpose" mirrors her excessive consumption beyond any reasonable need. A wrong answer that calls this "imagery" or "metaphor" without explaining the symbolic meaning shows the student can label the device but cannot interpret its thematic function.

questions.q: Analyze how the final revelation — "Today she weighs twenty-one stone" — functions as both situational irony and poetic justice. Support with two textual details.
questions.a: It is situational irony because the woman who preached moderation ("One should always get up from a meal feeling one could eat a little more") becomes the embodiment of excess (21 stone = 133 kg). It is poetic justice because the author, who suffered hunger and financial ruin from her gluttony, now sees her physically bear the consequence of her behaviour. Textual details: (1) her repeated claims of eating "only one thing" vs. the reality of her massive weight; (2) the author's closing tone of "complacency" observing the "result with complacency" after the "immortal gods take a hand." A weak answer that only notes she got fat misses the structural irony and thematic closure.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The restaurant Foyot's is merely a setting, not a symbol." Defend or refute using evidence from the text.
questions.a: Refute. Foyot's symbolizes the class divide and social pretension that trap the author. It is "where the French senators eat" — a space of power and privilege — and the author, a struggling writer, enters it only because he is "too young to have learned to say no to a woman." The restaurant's inflated prices (salmon, caviar, asparagus, peaches out of season) symbolize the exploitation of the vulnerable by the entitled. A student who agrees reveals a literal reading of setting, missing how physical spaces encode thematic conflicts in senior secondary literary analysis.

questions.q: Write a 4-sentence paragraph using PEEL structure explaining how the peach at the end of the luncheon symbolizes the woman's false innocence and the author's powerlessness.
questions.a: [Point] The peach offered at the end symbolizes the woman's performative innocence masking predatory exploitation. [Evidence] The headwaiter presents peaches with "the blush of an innocent girl" and "the rich tone of an Italian landscape," yet they are out of season and exorbitantly priced. [Explanation] Like the peach's deceptive beauty, the woman's charming conversation and dietary lectures conceal her calculated consumption of the author's limited means; she takes the peach "absentmindedly" after a massive meal, proving her indifference to cost. [Link] This moment crystallizes the story's central irony: the symbol of innocence becomes the final act of violation, leaving the author with "not a penny in my pocket" while she calls him a "humorist." A poor answer lists details without the PEEL chain or fails to connect symbol to theme.
